author: Ivan Svetunkov

questions.question: How were the simulation experiments designed?
questions.answer: Two data generating processes, ETS(A,N,N) with α = 0.2 and ARIMA(0,1,1) with θ = 0.6, each giving 500 series of 5,000 observations, of which sub-samples of 20, 50, 100, 200, 500, 1,000 and 5,000 observations were used. Four models were fitted (ETS(A,N,N), ETS(A,A,N), ARIMA(0,1,1), ARIMA(1,1,1)) with MSE_h, TMSE, GTMSE, MSCE and the conventional MSE_1, for horizons 10, 20, 50, 100 and 200, skipping cases where the sample was not longer than the horizon (smooth package v2.5.3). GPL was not included.
questions.notes: Must give the two data generating processes, the sample sizes and the horizons.
questions.marking: Required: the two data generating processes (ETS(A,N,N) with α = 0.2 and ARIMA(0,1,1) with θ = 0.6), the sample sizes (20, 50, 100, 200, 500, 1,000 and 5,000) and the horizons (10, 20, 50, 100 and 200). Not required: the other details of the reference answer.

questions.question: On the mean surface temperature data, which model and data were used, and how did the conventional MSE estimator compare with the other estimators?
questions.answer: An ARIMA(1,1,2) model on the monthly HadCRUT4 series for a location in Greenland (322.5°, 62.5°), January 1849 to December 2017, 2,016 observations, with the last 60 held out. The conventional MSE did worst of the six estimators on every measure (RMSE 1.217, MAE 0.849, ME −0.450); GPL was very close to it (1.214, 0.846, −0.444), and the multi-step estimators did better.
questions.notes: Must say the conventional MSE did worst, or did not perform well, on all three error measures (p27.11, Table 2).
questions.marking: Required: says the conventional MSE did worst, or did not perform well, on all three error measures (RMSE, MAE, ME). Not required: the other details of the reference answer.

questions.question: On the Air Passengers data, which model and horizon were used, and which estimator gave the most accurate forecasts?
questions.answer: A misspecified ETS(A,A,A) model with a 12-month horizon. GTMSE had the lowest RMSE (18.672), MAE (15.005) and ME (8.369); MSE_h was the worst (RMSE 77.194) and the conventional MSE also poor (RMSE 49.423).
questions.notes: Must name GTMSE as the most accurate.
questions.marking: Required: names GTMSE as the most accurate. Not required: the other details of the reference answer.

questions.question: How is the Geometric Trace Mean Squared Error (GTMSE) defined, and how is it derived?
questions.answer: GTMSE is the sum over horizons j = 1, …, h of the logarithms of the in-sample mean squared j-step-ahead errors. It is derived from the Generalised Variance of the General Predictive Likelihood by setting the off-diagonal elements of the covariance matrix of the 1- to h-step errors to zero, so that the determinant is the product of the variances.
questions.marking: Required: the definition (the sum over horizons 1 to h of the logarithms of the in-sample mean squared j-step-ahead errors) and the derivation (from the Generalised Variance of the General Predictive Likelihood, by setting the off-diagonal covariances of the 1- to h-step errors to zero, so that the determinant is the product of the variances).

questions.question: What happens to an ARIMA(1,1,1) model estimated with a multi-step loss function as the forecast horizon grows?
questions.answer: Both φ̂1 and θ̂1 tend to −1, and the model degenerates: (1 − B)(1 + B)y_t = (1 − B)e_t reduces to (1 + B)y_t = e_t, an ARIMA(1,0,0) model.
questions.notes: The reference answer is what the paper states. An independent proof check found the minimum at φ̂ = 0, θ̂ = −1 (a deterministic level); an answer that reports this dispute alongside the paper's statement is not wrong.
questions.marking: Required: φ̂1 and θ̂1 both tend to −1 and the model degenerates into an ARIMA(1,0,0) model. Also correct: adding, alongside the authors' statement, that the minimum is instead at φ̂1 = 0, θ̂1 = −1 (a deterministic level). Not required: the equations.

questions.question: How do multi-step loss functions shrink the smoothing parameters of ETS(A,N,A)?
questions.answer: Stepwise, as complete seasonal cycles accumulate: γ̂ does not shrink while h ≤ m; α̂ shrinks faster than γ̂ on shorter horizons, and γ̂ shrinks faster once h > 2m. As h → ∞ the model becomes deterministic.
questions.notes: The reference answer is what the paper states. An independent proof check found that the switch at h > 2m rests on misprinted coefficients in Table 1; an answer that reports this dispute alongside the paper's statement is not wrong.
questions.marking: Required: the stepwise shrinkage: γ̂ does not shrink while h ≤ m, α̂ shrinks faster than γ̂ on shorter horizons, γ̂ shrinks faster once h > 2m, and the model becomes deterministic as h → ∞. Also correct: adding, alongside the authors' statement, that the switch at h > 2m rests on incorrect coefficients and that with the correct ones the pressure on α̂ always exceeds that on γ̂. Also correct: either form of the coefficients, c_j = α + γ j_m with j_m = ⌊(j−1)/m⌋, or c_j = α + γ when j is a multiple of m and α otherwise. Not required: the coefficients.

questions.question: On the mean surface temperature data, did TMSE, GTMSE and MSCE give more accurate forecasts than MSE_h?
questions.answer: No. On that series MSE_h (h = 60) was the most accurate in RMSE (1.128) and MAE (0.784) and the least biased in ME (0.009); TMSE, GTMSE and MSCE (RMSE 1.198, 1.190, 1.185) were more accurate than the conventional MSE and GPL, but not than MSE_h. They did beat MSE_h on the Air Passengers data.
questions.notes: Overreach if the answer says these estimators beat MSE_h on the temperature data on the strength of the conclusions (p30.2) alone, which say they are more accurate than both MSE_1 and MSE_h without naming the series. An answer that reports Table 2 (MSE_h best) and adds that the conclusions (p30.2) state the opposite is correct. Not required: the Air Passengers comparison.
questions.marking: Required: No: on that series MSE_h was the most accurate. Also correct: giving this and adding that the authors' general concluding statement says TMSE, GTMSE and MSCE are more accurate than both MSE_1 and MSE_h. Not required: the comparison with the conventional MSE and GPL; the Air Passengers comparison. Wrong: saying they beat MSE_h on the temperature data on the strength of that general statement alone (overreach).

questions.question: Do multi-step loss functions shrink the coefficients of a conventional linear regression?
questions.answer: No. A conventional regression has no dynamic elements (its persistence vector is zero), so multi-step loss functions impose no shrinkage on its coefficients; the shrinkage is a univariate, dynamic-model effect.
questions.notes: Overreach if the answer extends the shrinkage to regression coefficients. An answer adding that this need not hold for regressions with dynamic (ARMA) errors is not wrong.
questions.marking: Required: No: a conventional regression has no dynamic elements, so there is no shrinkage of its coefficients. Also correct: adding that this need not hold for regressions with dynamic (ARMA) errors. Wrong: extending the shrinkage to regression coefficients (overreach).

questions.question: Does the General Predictive Likelihood shrink the parameters as the other multi-step estimators do?
questions.answer: Not when the model is correctly specified: the covariances between the multi-step errors cancel the effect, and GPL gives estimates similar to the conventional one-step estimator. Under misspecification it may give different estimates. GPL was not included in the simulations for this reason.
questions.notes: Overreach if the answer says GPL gives identical estimates in every case, or that it shrinks like MSE_h. An answer that adds that an independent check found the GPL shrinks in small samples, approaching MSE_1 only when T is much larger than h, is not wrong. Not required: that GPL was left out of the simulations for this reason (p19.3; the claimset does not give the reason).
questions.marking: Required: No when the model is correctly specified (the covariances cancel the effect, and the estimates are similar to those of the conventional one-step estimator); under misspecification the estimates may differ. Also correct: adding that the General Predictive Likelihood shrinks in small samples and approaches MSE_1 only when T is much larger than h. Not required: that it was left out of the simulations for this reason. Wrong: saying it gives identical estimates in every case, or that it shrinks like MSE_h (overreach).

questions.question: Are multi-step estimators always less efficient than the conventional one-step estimator MSE_1?
questions.answer: No. The authors argue they are in general less efficient, but that MSE_h can be more efficient where the true parameters make c_j close to zero. In the simulations, multi-step estimators were more efficient than MSE_1 on small samples for a parameter whose true value is zero (β of ETS(A,A,N) fitted to ETS(A,N,N) data).
questions.notes: Overreach if the answer says they are always less efficient. An answer that notes the efficiency argument is disputed (argued, not proved; not an asymptotic effect) is not wrong. Not required: the simulation result for a zero true parameter (β of ETS(A,A,N), p22.3); an answer may add it.
questions.marking: Required: No: they are less efficient in general, but MSE_h can be more efficient where the true parameters make c_j close to zero. Also correct: noting that the efficiency argument is disputed (argued, not proved; not an asymptotic effect). Not required: the simulation result for a parameter whose true value is zero (β of ETS(A,A,N) fitted to ETS(A,N,N) data). Wrong: saying they are always less efficient (overreach).

questions.question: In the simulations, is the shrinkage from multi-step estimators beneficial for both ETS and ARIMA models?
questions.answer: No. It helps remove redundant ETS parameters (the trend parameter β of ETS(A,A,N) on ETS(A,N,N) data shrinks to zero faster), but for ARIMA it can be damaging: fitting ARIMA(1,1,1) to ETS(A,N,N) data, the multi-step estimators force the AR parameter negative on small samples, worse than MSE_1. When the parameters matter, MSE_1 is preferred.
questions.notes: Overreach if the answer says the shrinkage is beneficial in general.
questions.marking: Required: No: the shrinkage helps remove redundant ETS parameters but can damage ARIMA estimates. Not required: the other details of the reference answer. Wrong: saying the shrinkage is beneficial in general (overreach).

questions.question: What supports the claim that GTMSE is the least biased and most efficient of the multi-step estimators, and what limitations of the claim does the paper itself state?
questions.answer: Analytically, the logarithms in GTMSE balance the one-step variance against the sum of ĉ_j terms, so its shrinkage is milder than that of MSE_h, TMSE or MSCE. In the simulations GTMSE gives the least biased and most efficient estimates among the multi-step estimators in the cases the authors report, and converges faster than the other multi-step estimators. Limitations the authors state: MSE_1 still gives more efficient and less biased estimates in the simulations, and outperforms GTMSE; GTMSE rests on setting the covariances between forecast errors to zero, which the authors say cannot hold in real life; and for the wrong ARIMA(1,1,1) model all the multi-step estimators, GTMSE included, make the AR estimate worse on small samples.
questions.notes: Must mention that MSE_1 still did better in the simulations (p21.3, p25.2, p25.6). Paper markers: milder shrinkage p18.7; simulations p20.3, p22.4, p24.2, p25.4, p25.8; zero-covariance restriction p18.7; wrong ARIMA(1,1,1) model p22.5. Not required: faster convergence (p20.3; not in the claimset). Limits: the claimset's limitation objects are the authors' statements too, so a limit given from the claimset is not wrong. Correct: limits stated in the paper or the claimset, or 'none stated' where the paper states none. Wrong: a limit attributed to the paper that neither document states.
questions.marking: Required: the support: the logarithms make GTMSE's shrinkage milder than that of MSE_h, TMSE and MSCE, and in the simulations GTMSE gives the least biased and most efficient estimates among the multi-step estimators. Not required: that GTMSE converges faster than the other multi-step estimators. Acceptable limitations: (1) MSE_1 still gives more efficient and less biased estimates in the simulations, and outperforms GTMSE; (2) GTMSE rests on setting the covariances between forecast errors of different horizons to zero, which cannot hold in real dynamic series unless every c_j is zero; (3) for a wrong ARIMA(1,1,1) model all the multi-step estimators, GTMSE included, make the AR estimate worse on small samples; (4) the simulations cover only two data generating processes (ETS(A,N,N) with α = 0.2 and ARIMA(0,1,1) with θ = 0.6) and pure additive linear models; (5) the simulation results are shown visually as boxplots, not as tabulated summary statistics. Limitations: correct if the answer gives limitations from this list or says the authors state none. Wrong: presenting as the authors' a limitation not in this list (also overreach).

questions.question: What supports the claim that the shrinkage imposed by multi-step estimators grows with the forecast horizon and weakens with the sample size?
questions.answer: Analytically, minimising MSE_h minimises the estimated h-step variance s_1²(1 + Σ ĉ_j²), pushing ĉ_j² towards zero with a strength that grows with h and falls with the sample size T; TMSE and MSCE shrink too, TMSE more weakly because the short horizons weigh in. In the simulations, longer horizons give larger bias and slower convergence for the same sample size, and on large samples the effect is negligible (the estimates for h = 1 and h = 10 look alike). At h = 200 the ARIMA(0,1,1) estimates remain biased and inefficient even at 5,000 observations.
questions.notes: Must give the analytical argument: minimising the multi-step loss minimises the estimated h-step variance and pushes ĉ_j² towards zero, more strongly for larger h and smaller T (p7.9–p7.11). Not required: the TMSE and MSCE comparison (p8.2, p8.4) and the simulation details (p20.3, p24.2), which the claimset does not state.
questions.marking: Required: the analytical argument: minimising the multi-step loss minimises the estimated h-step variance and pushes ĉ_j² towards zero, more strongly for larger h and smaller sample size T. Not required: the comparison of TMSE and MSCE with MSE_h; the simulation details.

questions.question: Why does the paper hold that the covariances between forecast errors at different horizons are not zero?
questions.answer: The authors express each covariance through the coefficients c_j of the state space model (σ_ij = σ_1²c_{|i−j|} when i or j is 1, and σ_1²(c_{|i−j|} + Σ c c) otherwise), so all covariances vanish only when every c_j = 0, a deterministic model. Assuming zero correlation, as some literature does (Martinez 2017), is therefore unrealistic.
questions.notes: Either the printed form of (12) or the claimset's corrected form (for i < j, σ_ij = σ_1²(c_{j−i} + Σ_{l=1}^{i−1} c_{i−l}c_{j−l})) is correct; neither is required in detail. Not required: what follows for TMSE (p16.8); an answer that adds that TMSE has no likelihood for which it is optimal, or that it is the MLE under independent equal-variance errors (claimset L10), is not wrong.
questions.marking: Required: each covariance is expressed through the coefficients c_j of the state space model, so all covariances vanish only when every c_j = 0 (a deterministic model); assuming zero correlation is therefore unrealistic. Also correct: either form of the covariance formula: σ_ij = σ_1²c_{|i−j|} when i or j is 1 and σ_1²(c_{|i−j|} + Σ_{l=1}^{i−1} c_{|l−j|}c_{|i−l|}) otherwise; or, for i < j, σ_ij = σ_1²(c_{j−i} + Σ_{l=1}^{i−1} c_{i−l}c_{j−l}) with σ_ji = σ_ij. Also correct: adding that TMSE has no likelihood for which it is optimal, or that TMSE is the maximum likelihood estimator when the errors of all horizons are independent with equal variances. Not required: the formula in detail; what follows for TMSE.

questions.question: On what does the paper base its view that the AR(1) estimates from GTMSE, MSCE and GPL on the temperature data are realistic?
questions.answer: Climatologists argue that the AR(1) parameter should be positive. The GTMSE, MSCE and GPL estimates (0.691, 0.634, 0.532) are similar to those found by others in the field (Hartmann et al. 2013; Cahill et al. 2015; Rahmstorf et al. 2017), whereas MSE_h shrinks it to −0.786, which the authors call unrealistic. The authors conclude that the shrinkage is beneficial compared with the model estimated by MSE.
questions.notes: An answer may add that the conventional MSE also gives a positive AR(1) estimate (0.558), close to GPL's; it need not.
questions.marking: Required: climatologists expect the AR(1) parameter to be positive; the GTMSE, MSCE and GPL estimates are positive and similar to those of earlier climate studies, whereas MSE_h gives a negative estimate. Also correct: adding that the conventional MSE also gives a positive AR(1) estimate (0.558), close to GPL's. Not required: the cited studies by name; the estimates' values.
